title: Part A – SQL Analysis
text:
SQL Query

List the total budget allocated for productions in each country
along with the count of projects per country
sorted by total budget (descending)


query_budget_country <- "
SELECT 
  c.Country AS Country,
  COUNT(p.ProductionID) AS Number_of_Productions,
  SUM(p.Budget) AS Total_Budget
FROM Productions p
JOIN Clients c
  ON p.ClientID = c.ClientID
GROUP BY c.Country
ORDER BY Total_Budget DESC
"

budget_country_df <- dbGetQuery(con, query_budget_country)

## Display Results as a Paginated Table

datatable(
  budget_country_df,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 8,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
)

title: Part A – SQL Analysis
text:
Explanation
This query joins the Productions and Clients tables to aggregate production budgets by country. The total budget and number of productions are calculated using SUM and COUNT, and the results are sorted in descending order of total budget to highlight countries with the highest investment in virtual production.

Explanation 1st query
This query joins the Productions and Clients tables to aggregate production budgets by country. The total budget and number of productions are calculated using SUM and COUNT, and the results are sorted in descending order of total budget to highlight countries with the highest investment in virtual production.

query_avg_dev_time <- "
SELECT
  AssetCount,
  AVG(DevelopmentDays) AS Avg_Development_Days
FROM (
  SELECT
    p.ProductionID,
    JULIANDAY(p.EndDate) - JULIANDAY(p.StartDate) AS DevelopmentDays,
    COUNT(a.AssetID) AS AssetCount
  FROM Productions p
  LEFT JOIN Environments e
    ON p.ProductionID = e.ProductionID
  LEFT JOIN Assets a
    ON e.EnvironmentID = a.EnvironmentID
  GROUP BY p.ProductionID
)
GROUP BY AssetCount
ORDER BY AssetCount
"

avg_dev_time_df <- dbGetQuery(con, query_avg_dev_time)

## Display as a Paginated Table


datatable(
  avg_dev_time_df,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 8,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
)

title: Part A – SQL Analysis
text:
Explanation 2nd query
This query calculates the development duration for each production by subtracting the start date from the end date using SQLite’s JULIANDAY function. A subquery is used to count the number of assets associated with each production. The outer query then groups productions by asset count and computes the average development time, highlighting how asset volume relates to production duration.

query_top_crew <- "
SELECT
  cm.Name AS Crew_Member,
  COUNT(p.ProductionID) AS Successful_Productions
FROM CrewMembers cm
JOIN ProductionCrew pc
  ON cm.CrewID = pc.CrewID
JOIN Productions p
  ON pc.ProductionID = p.ProductionID
WHERE p.Status IN ('Post-production', 'Completed')
GROUP BY cm.CrewID, cm.Name
ORDER BY Successful_Productions DESC
LIMIT 3
"

top_crew_df <- dbGetQuery(con, query_top_crew)

## Display the Results

datatable(
  top_crew_df,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 3,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
)

title: Part A – SQL Analysis
text:
Explanation 3rd query
This query identifies the top three crew members based on their involvement in successful productions. Success is defined as productions with a status of *Post-production* or *Completed*. The query joins crew members to productions via the production–crew linking table, aggregates the number of successful productions per crew member, and orders the results in descending order to highlight the most experienced contributors.

title: Part A – SQL Analysis
text:
1st concept
Filter using LIKE combine conditions with OR

Example scenario
List crew members whose role contains Unreal or Camera

query_like_or <- "
SELECT
  Name,
  Role,
  ExperienceYears
FROM CrewMembers
WHERE Role LIKE '%Unreal%'
   OR Role LIKE '%Camera%'
"

like_or_df <- dbGetQuery(con, query_like_or)

### Display the Table

datatable(
  like_or_df,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
)







Explanation 1st concept
This query demonstrates the use of the LIKE operator combined with the OR condition to filter textual data. Crew members are selected if their role contains either the term Unreal or Camera, allowing flexible pattern matching across multiple criteria.

title: Part A – SQL Analysis
text:
2nd concept
Filter using SELECT DISTINCT with ORDER BY

Example scenario
List distinct production genres in alphabetical order

query_distinct_order <- "
SELECT DISTINCT
  Genre
FROM Productions
ORDER BY Genre ASC
"

distinct_genres_df <- dbGetQuery(con, query_distinct_order)

### Display Table

datatable(
  distinct_genres_df,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
)







Explanation 2nd concept
This query uses `SELECT DISTINCT` to return unique production genres, eliminating duplicate values. The `ORDER BY` clause sorts the results alphabetically, improving readability and supporting categorical analysis.

title: Part A – SQL Analysis
text:
3rd concept
Subquery with SELECT

Example scenario
List productions whose budget is above the average budget

query_subquery <- "
SELECT
  Title,
  Budget
FROM Productions
WHERE Budget > (
  SELECT AVG(Budget)
  FROM Productions
)
ORDER BY Budget DESC
"

above_avg_budget_df <- dbGetQuery(con, query_subquery)


### Display Table

datatable(
  above_avg_budget_df,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
)







Explanation 3rd concept
This query uses a subquery to calculate the average production budget. The outer query then filters productions whose budget exceeds this average, illustrating how subqueries can be used to perform comparative analysis within SQL.

title: Part B – Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Introduction
This section applies linear regression analysis to examine how production budget and crew size influence the success rate of virtual productions. The aim is to identify trends, interpret model coefficients, and evaluate the reliability of the regression model.

library(DBI)

Warning: package 'DBI' was built under R version 4.5.2

library(RSQLite)

Warning: package 'RSQLite' was built under R version 4.5.2

library(ggplot2)

Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.5.2

## Connect to the SQLite database
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  RSQLite::SQLite(),
  "virtual_production.db"
)

## Check tables exist and we are connected to the DB

dbListTables(con)

 [1] "Assets"           "Clients"          "CrewMembers"      "Environments"    
 [5] "Equipment"        "ProductionCrew"   "Productions"      "SessionEquipment"
 [9] "ShootingSessions" "VCamTakes"       




Model
This section performs linear regression to predict the success rate of a production based on its budget and crew size and present the data in an appropriate plot

## Build the Regression Dataset (SQL)

query_regression <- "
SELECT
  p.Budget,
  COUNT(pc.CrewID) AS CrewSize,
  CASE
    WHEN p.Status IN ('Completed', 'Post-production') THEN 1
    ELSE 0
  END AS SuccessRate
FROM Productions p
LEFT JOIN ProductionCrew pc
  ON p.ProductionID = pc.ProductionID
GROUP BY p.ProductionID, p.Budget, p.Status
"

regression_data <- dbGetQuery(con, query_regression)

## Perform the Linear Regression

model <- lm(SuccessRate ~ Budget + CrewSize, data = regression_data)
summary(model)


Call:
lm(formula = SuccessRate ~ Budget + CrewSize, data = regression_data)

Residuals:

---

Residual standard error: 0.3254 on 3 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7883,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6471 
F-statistic: 5.585 on 2 and 3 DF,  p-value: 0.09742




Interpret
This section interprets the model coefficients and discuss what insights they provide about cinematic production.

## Plot the Data (Required Task #2)

ggplot(regression_data, aes(x = Budget, y = SuccessRate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Success Rate vs Production Budget",
    x = "Budget",
    y = "Success Rate"
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Final comments
The regression model examines how production budget and crew size relate to the success rate of virtual productions. A positive budget suggests that higher-budget productions are more likely to be successful. The crew size coefficient in the same way indicates whether larger teams are associated with higher success rates.
The reliability of the model is limited by the definition of success rate. Also, productions with unusually high budgets may influence the regression results. So, the model provides general trends rather than precise predictions.
